lesson.title: Polynomials: The Best-Behaved Functions in Calculus
lesson.summary: Polynomials are continuous at every real number, a fact that follows directly from the limit laws and makes them the natural starting point for understanding continuity.
lesson.body:
When you trace the graph of a polynomial with a pencil, you never have to lift the pencil off the paper. That simple physical fact captures the essence of continuity: a function is continuous at a point when its graph has no jump, no hole, and no break there. Polynomials, functions built entirely from adding and multiplying powers of x with real coefficients, turn out to be continuous at every single real number. This is not a coincidence that needs to be checked case by case. It follows directly from the definition of a continuous function and the basic limit laws you already know, and it explains why polynomials are the natural starting point whenever a course introduces continuity.

The proof rests on two extremely simple building blocks. First, a constant function f(x) = c is continuous everywhere, since its limit at any point a is just c, which equals f(a). Second, the identity function f(x) = x is continuous everywhere, since the limit of x as x approaches a is simply a, which equals f(a). Every polynomial, no matter how complicated, is built from these two pieces using only addition, subtraction, and multiplication. The limit laws tell you that the limit of a sum is the sum of the limits, and the limit of a product is the product of the limits, as long as each piece has a limit. Chaining these laws together, term by term, shows that the limit of a polynomial at any point a is obtained simply by substituting x = a into the formula.

This gives the general theorem: if p(x) is any polynomial function, then p is continuous at every real number a, meaning the limit of p(x) as x approaches a equals p(a), for all a. Because a is arbitrary, this is the same as saying a polynomial is continuous on its entire domain, which is all real numbers. Practically, this means you never need to build a table of values or worry about one-sided limits when evaluating a limit of a polynomial. You just substitute the number directly.

Consider f(x) = 3x^3 - 2x^2 + 5 at x = 2. Direct substitution gives f(2) = 3(8) - 2(4) + 5 = 24 - 8 + 5 = 21. To confirm this matches the limit, break the polynomial into pieces: the limit of 3x^3 as x approaches 2 is 3(2)^3 = 24, the limit of -2x^2 is -2(2)^2 = -8, and the limit of the constant 5 is 5. Adding these three limits gives 24 - 8 + 5 = 21, exactly matching f(2). Since the two values agree, f is continuous at x = 2, and the same reasoning works at every other real number, since nothing about the argument depended on the specific value 2.

This result matters beyond polynomials themselves. It is the first domino in a chain: once you know polynomials are continuous everywhere, the quotient rule for limits extends continuity to rational functions wherever the denominator is nonzero, which is the next topic. It also underlies why so many calculus techniques, from the Intermediate Value Theorem to basic curve sketching, apply so cleanly to polynomial models. Continuity is what allows you to trust that small changes in x produce small changes in output, and polynomials give you that guarantee everywhere, with no exceptions and no fine print.
